zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the transcription.

runs.text: Eſtarem os pès do caualo como

lines.note: Sucunda continues the preceding entry's principal forms. The Portuguese begins the literal sense: a horse's feet become stiff or unable to move; the continuation is indented, not a new entry.
The feet are incapacitated so that the horse cannot walk. Permet. introduces a figurative use, and Fi- begins Fito on the following line.
Fitono mayede sucunde voru describes freezing or shrinking back in front of people. The historical voru is retained; dian- continues as diante below.

runs.text: te de gẽte comoatado, & encolhido ſem poder

lines.note: The figurative subject stands before others as though bound and cowering. The print joins comoatado; the tilde in gẽte is not expanded.
Completes the figurative explanation: unable to do anything. This short indented continuation closes the preceding entry.
Sucumo is identified with nuka, the husk or bran of grain. The scan's m corrects OCR Sucuino; tri- starts Portuguese trigo rather than another Japanese form.
Completes trigo, adding wheat and other grains to the rice-husk definition. The physical division tri-/go is retained.
Sucunai means few or little in quantity. The compact Portuguese gloss directly supplies that sense.
Sucunasa is the corresponding nominal form, the smallness of a quantity or scarcity. It belongs to the preceding adjective rather than carrying a separate Portuguese gloss.
Sucunoo and sucunacu are the two printed adverbial forms. The caron and the connecting l are retained rather than replacing them with modern spelling or an expanded Latin label.
Sucure is the verb for becoming stiff or cramped; Meliùs recommends Sucumi as the preferable form. The abbreviated principal parts remain as printed.
Uma no ashi ga sucureta gives a horse's feet becoming stiff. The scan supports Vmano axiga, correcting the malformed OCR and its derived kana hint; the gloss continues below.

runs.text: caualo como hirtos, ou tropegos de não andar,

lines.note: Completes the subject, the horse, and describes its feet as stiff or halting from lack of movement. The visible letters support caualo, not OCR caialo; the row is a continuation.

runs.text: ou eſtar muito tempo na eſtrebaria ſem ſajr.

lines.note: The alternative cause is a long stay in the stable without going out. The historical eſtrebaria and ſajr are preserved rather than modernized.
Sucuyacana describes a strong or vigorous person. The Portuguese word is Peßoa despite worn spacing around its last letters; the Japanese historical vowel sequence is retained.
These supply the adverbial and nominal forms of the preceding adjective: vigorously and vigor or robustness. They are Japanese forms, not embedded Portuguese terms.
Sudachi concerns birds leaving the nest. The final principal part is visibly weak and spaced as da ta; that chosen reading is retained rather than silently supplying the expected doubled t.
Completes the fledging sense by specifying departure from the nest for the first time. This is not the unrelated citrus name with the same modern romanization.
The nominal entry gives sudachi wo suru, to make that first departure from the nest. Idem points back to the preceding verb's definition.
Sudai is explained through kazu no yo as many ages or generations. The worn word in the Portuguese is Muitas, not two independent words Mu tas.
Sudaqi denotes insects sounding together. The Japanese form and the scan's damaged u support Sudaqi rather than Sidaqi; co- begins como below.
Completes como grilos, giving crickets as the example of insects calling together. The short continuation closes Sudaqi.

runs.text: Eſteira rala que ſe dependura às portas

lines.note: Sudare is an open or loosely woven hanging blind. The visible final re corrects Sadate; the Portuguese says it is hung at doorways.
The blind may also hang on verandas. Sudare goxi- begins the expression for speaking through or across such a screen, completed on the next row.
Sudare goshi ni kotoba wo kawasu means exchanging words through a blind. The Portuguese begins speaking while having something between the speakers; tẽ- continues below.

runs.text: do entre meo algũa eſteira deſtas.

lines.note: Completes tendo: one of these blinds stands between the speakers. Both the historical meo and the tilde carrier in algũa are retained.

runs.text: Adu. Ia ja, ou quaſi ja a ponto, em-

lines.note: Sudeni is labelled an adverb and explained here as already or almost at the point of something. The scan has a word space in quaſi ja; em- continues with perigo.
The gloss adds being in danger and gives an example of nearly dying. Itaita is retained as the historical form, not modernized to itashita; the Portuguese makes the near-death sense explicit.

runs.text: Eſteue ja quaſi a ponto de morrer.

lines.note: The example means that someone was already almost at the point of death. This establishes the imminent or narrowly avoided sense in this use of Sudeni.
Sudeni faya adds the Japanese reinforcing element haya and is referred back to the same explanation by Idem.
Sudo is the expression for many times, paraphrased by kazu no tabi. Its final o is left unaccented as printed.
Sufada is glossed as bare or without armor. Sufadamu- begins the compound for an unarmored warrior on the following line.
Xa completes sufadamuxa, an unarmored soldier. The next example starts sufada ni; its u is supported by the scan rather than OCR Safadani.
Gusoku wo kiru completes the example: put armor directly on the bare body. The Portuguese armas here is explained by the clothing context, not by carrying a weapon in the hand.

runs.text: carnes nũas ſem vestido de baixo.

lines.note: Completes the example as armor over bare flesh, with no clothing underneath. The printed short s in vestido is retained.
This Sufai concerns numerous people or companions, paraphrased by kazu no tomogara. It is distinct from the following homograph about drinking cups.
Completes the first Sufai gloss with persons as an alternative to men. It belongs to the people-counting sense.
This homograph counts drinking cups: kazu no sakazuki. The Portuguese explanation begins many servings or rounds and continues with wine below.

The example concerns receiving several cups and becoming drunk, as the following gloss explains. Sufai is retained as the preferred reading of the abraded first word; its u is weak, unlike the clear headword above.

runs.text: Bebendo muitas vezes, ou copos de vinho em

lines.note: The Portuguese explains repeated drinking or drinking several cups of wine. Its final em belongs to embebedarſe on the next physical row, although no terminal hyphen is printed.
Completes embebedarſe, becoming drunk. The physical division after em is retained without supplying a hyphen.

runs.text: Ienjiure em vinagre, l, em achar.

lines.note: Sufajicami is ginger in vinegar or pickle. The damaged final noun is read as achar, with a faint c and an italic h, rather than OCR alhar; this remains a nonblocking reading caveat. Lexical corroboration: Porto Editora, Infopédia, s.v. achar (culinary noun), which defines a vinegar-based preserve; consulted 2 October 2026.
Sufenno qioo denotes several sections or volumes of scripture or books. The printed caron in qiǒ is preserved; the Portuguese sentence continues with liuros.
Completes the book-section sense, then introduces the separate sense many times. Sufen me- starts an example about repeated servings, with the damaged vowel read as e rather than OCR o.
Mexi and saqe are rice or a meal and wine arriving repeatedly. The Portuguese has vinho, correcting OCR citho; xi completes the divided mexi.
Adds rice and so forth to the things repeatedly brought. This continuation completes the Sufen example.
Sufiacu means many hundreds, paraphrased by kazu no hyaku. The scan supports Sufiacu and fiacu, not the malformed Sanacu and fiucu in the OCR.
Sufin names the first or principal disciple. The gloss supplies the institutional sense without requiring a modernized spelling of the Japanese title.

runs.text: Certa erua de que fazem minos, l, cha-

lines.note: Suga is a plant used to make rain capes or hats. Minos is a Japanese word incorporated into the Portuguese explanation, unlike the separate entry forms.
Completes chapeos, then defines sugagomo as a mat made from this plant. The Japanese compound begins a new sense within the same entry block.
Completes the material description: the mat is made from that plant. No species identification is imposed beyond the source's erua.
Sugame means looking askance or squinting. The scan supports torto with final o, rather than OCR torta.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Fechar hum pouco os olhos pera ver

lines.note: A further sense is partly closing the eyes in order to see. The purpose of narrowing the eyes continues on the following row.

runs.text: milhor, ou ver ſe está algũa couſa direita. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the purpose as seeing better or checking whether something is straight. Milhor is the printed historical form; enlarged reinspection resolves the mark in está as an acute accent, not the OCR's tilde.
Me wo sugamete miru means looking with narrowed eyes. Idem refers to the just-described act rather than introducing a different object.

runs.text: Torto de hũ olho, ou o que olhade

lines.note: The noun describes someone with a defective or misaligned eye, or one who looks askance. The scan has hũ and the joined olhade, retained without expanding the abbreviation or adding a space.
Completes the alternative description of looking sideways or askance. This closes the eye-related noun before the vinegar-vessel homograph.
Sugame and sutsubo are vessels for vinegar. Boyão is the printed Portuguese jar term, correcting garbled OCR Biãs; vina- continues below.
Completes vinagre, vinegar. This short physical row belongs to the vessel definition, not to Sugamino below.

runs.text: Capa de agoa que ſe faz da erua

lines.note: Sugamino is a rain cape made from the plant named on the next line. The Portuguese agoa is left in its historical spelling.
Completes the definition by naming the plant Suga. Here Suga is embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is eligible for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Caniçada que ſe faz de bambus.

lines.note: Sugaqi is a bamboo lattice or fence. The gloss identifies the material directly and does not require a particular construction beyond caniçada.
The corresponding verb means spreading or stretching something in a lattice-like way. The comparison with spiders begins in the divided Portuguese a-/ranhas.

runs.text: ranhas a tea à maneira de caniçada. ¶

lines.note: Spiders extend their web like a lattice. Ca- begins Caje, wind, in the Japanese example on the following line.
The example describes a spider spreading its threads before the wind. The scan supports ſaſaganino, not OCR ſaſagonino; the comparison remains unfinished until gotoxi below.

runs.text: Como aranha que faz a tea exposta

lines.note: Gotoxi completes the Japanese comparison, like a spider making a web. The Portuguese specifies that the web is exposed, with the complement below.
Completes the comparison: the spider's web is exposed to the wind. This closes the example attached to the verb Sugaqi.
Sugara is illustrated in michi sugara, along the way. The Portuguese Pello caminho supplies the spatial, continuous sense.
Yomosugara illustrates the temporal counterpart, all night. The joined Portuguese anoite is preserved as printed.
Sugari means leaning or resting against something. The printed comma after Arrimarſe is retained along with the abbreviated principal parts.
Tsue ni sugaru means leaning on a staff. The scan supports ni rather than OCR ui; bor- begins bordão below.
Completes bordão, then gives clinging to a sleeve or its hanging portion. A- begins Portuguese Aferrar on the next row.

runs.text: ferrar das mangas, ou pegarſe nellas.

lines.note: Completes Aferrar and explains grasping or clinging to the sleeves. The two Japanese sleeve words belong to the preceding example.
Sugaritsuki is the compound verb for clinging or attaching oneself. Idem refers to the leaning or grasping sense just given.
This distinct Sugari concerns a season ending or passing. The printed gatta differs from the earlier atta and is preserved rather than regularized.
Completes tempo and gives melons going out of season as the example. The printed dalgũa and fruita remain unchanged.
Completes the Portuguese statement that melon season passes. Ichiga tachi begins a market-related example; ichi, market, and the visible ch correct OCR Ieniga.

runs.text: Acabarſe a feira, ou auer pouca gẽ-

lines.note: Completes ichi ga tachi sugaru: the market is ending or has few people left. The terminal Japanese vowel is read as u, consistent with the visible form and the example's verb.
Completes the divided gẽ-/tea and the statement about people remaining at the fair. The apparently superfluous a in tea is retained as printed; it is not silently reduced to gente ja.
Sugata means figure or form. This short independent entry is distinct from both the preceding verb and the following fitting-in verb.
Sugue and xisugue denote fitting or inserting a part into another. The Portuguese comparison begins co-/mo below.

runs.text: mo hastea de lança no ferro, &c.

lines.note: The example is fitting a spear shaft into its iron head. Hastea is retained as the printed historical form, not rewritten to modern haste.
This Sugue, alternatively suga, is the plant used for hats and rain capes. The scan supports Sugue rather than the OCR's Sague.
Completes the list of uses for the plant with rain capes. This belongs to the plant entry rather than the fitting-in verb above.
Sugegasa are hats made from the plant just described. The source's plural Portuguese gloss is preserved.
Suguenai means harsh or unpleasing. The damaged vowel in pouco is read as u, not the OCR's poaco.
Applied to a person, suguenai denotes harshness or an unresponsive, cold manner. Riſpido corrects OCR riſoido and agrees with the adjective in the preceding gloss.
Applied to a tree, the adjective concerns an unpleasing appearance. A- begins apraziuel, and the Portuguese distinguishes wood or a tree without modern botanical terminology.
Completes apraziuel and the tree's description as lacking a pleasing or graceful appearance. The printed coordination is retained without rewriting its syntax.
Suguenasa is the corresponding noun, harshness or unattractiveness. It remains an indented derivative of the adjective.
Suguenoo is the adverb, equated with nasakenoo. Both printed carons are preserved, and the explanatory i, belongs to the roman material rather than an isolated italic comma.
Completes seca and glosses the manner as coldly or harshly. The row closes the adjective's derivative forms.
Suguet means many months, paraphrased with tsuki. Its final t is the printed checked ending and is not expanded to tçu; the Portuguese begins moons or months.
Completes the Portuguese alternative meses, months. The damaged long s corrects OCR me es; the catchword below is separate page furniture.
The catchword is separated from the signature and the right-hand rule. The visible short form Sugu. is retained, although the next page begins Sugui; no missing i is silently supplied.
